item.content:encoded:
edit: edits made

The WikiWalk team is proposing edits to this page. All proposed edits will be in a collapsible below this post, and after 7 days if there are no serious objections to the edits, the feedback received will be taken into account as the edits are made. If you have questions not directly related to the article about this project, please pm a member of the WikiWalk Team.

+ Show
- Hide

To link to another article that creates a short time loop via use, I propose the following edit:

It is believed that when SCP-292 is flipped over, a process is started in which, if SCP-292 is flipped again before its sands run out, time flows in reverse to a point a couple of seconds before SCP-292 was initially flipped.

to

It is believed that when SCP-292 is flipped over, a process is started in which, if SCP-292 is flipped again before its sands run out, time flows in reverse to a point a couple of seconds before SCP-292 was initially flipped.1

Footnotes
1. This effect is similar in nature to that of SCP-1876, albeit with different psychological effects on those experiencing the phenomenon.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
If it has a self-preservation method against being shattered, it's likely to have prevented an destruction-of-eveything-end-of-the-world event (XK-class). After all, the destruction of the Earth would likely result in the destruction of the hourglass.

However, if it has done this in the past, how did Earth get unstuck from the time-loop? What would have stopped the scenario from unfolding as it did? If a researcher in the foundation suddenly 'felt like something bad would happen if I did so-and-so', that could definitely prevent the scenario. But what if it was a meteorite?

I believe that 292 may have been created as a device for stopping stupid mistakes made by the foundation that would result in the end of the world. The deja-vu feeling would make any researcher about to destroy the world suddenly take pause and not do the action, though this would only apply to scenarios that would destroy the world in a few seconds.

I have to admit that I adore this SCP despite its low recognition and 100- rating.

item.title: Re: An experiment, that might be a bad idea
item.content:encoded:
682 has never displayed any time-altering abilities, so I highly doubt that he would be able to 1) recognize what was going on (though it's quite possible that he could; the egg timer/hourglass exudes a heavy 'deja vu' (sorry for the lack of accents) effect, after all) and 2) react to it. If he gets sent back in time to just before the hourglass is turned, his actions up until that point will not have taken place. He could, possibly, adapt himself over the course of, I don't know, hundreds of thousands of 'hourglass revolutions', but adaptations usually take at least an hour and have been shown to take up to three days to complete. Given that he only has about, what, two seconds (if the clockwork is going at a maximum speed that wouldn't subject the sands to the centripetal/centrifugal effects) each time, adaptation that take place after the effects of the hourglass take place would reset each time, though it is possible that the increased urgency and relative ease of the adaptation could result in him, eventually, doing what you have described. It's also possible that, because just after three rotations, the hourglass exuded intense amounts of hallucinogenic effects, it could begin to spread these effects throughout, first, the Foundation, and second, the world. This, coupled with the very fast reset time would most likely render 682 useless/unable to think. The prolonged (3+ turns) effects of it are undocumented and may result in death due to, I don't know, seizure, after five or six turns.

In short: he'd be reset so quickly that an adaptation is incredibly unlikely, though he may realize what's going on. After a few turns, though, the psychological/physical effects of the hourglass may end up spreading farther and influencing 682 (and the rest of everyone).

I think that it's far more likely that an SCP such as 343 would 1) be unaffected and 2) notice that something was going wrong with the universe, though 343 has not specifically been tested against anomalous time affecting devices.

Perhaps 343 should come in and turn the timer. I'd like to see that.

item.title: An experiment, that might be a bad idea
item.content:encoded:
I was gonna ask what would happen if you attached it to a clockwork (or electrical or whatever) device that would start turning it some seconds after activation, giving whoever activated it enough time to move out of the deja vu range, and keep turning it again every N seconds. But then I realized this experiment would never be approved due to the risk of trapping the whole world into a time loop.

Though perhaps the universe would be saved by 682 because he got pissed the people he had just killed kept coming back alive again and again, and so broke thru the walls cycle after cycle until managing to get to it fast enough to destroy it, or at least the turning machine, before the next rewind?

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded: Thanks. And no, that did make sense, except that we do know what happens when it's flipped and allowed to run out. But we have no clue how it rewinds time. Heck, we have no way to observe 292 while it's rewinding. A lot of what is "known" about 292 is speculated or, at best, inferred.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
One of the things I like about this one is that barring some sort of fixed-in-the-time-stream-relative-to-something-not-affected-by-this object, it seem impossible to figure out what exactly happened while the timer was flipped. For all we know, flipping the timer summons a shiny black demon that incinerates all in the immediate area, feels guilty, and rewinds time by itself, or dropping it summons the Interactive Fiction genie ala the 'do not break' glass cube.

Or maybe I'm just rambling because I haven't slept. Regardless, even though rewinding time is a little cliche, I still like how it's set out and think the experiments with it still show promise.

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded: Thanks, y'all. That is one big difference with 688, in that you could (easily) use 292 for personal gain. But, you can't just have something go wrong and then flip it. 292 doesn't start recording till it's flipped, then you've got 60 seconds to rewind before the sand runs out. It'd be better used just before a short, high-risk activity, then if it fails, flip back over and rewind. Also, potentially, precognition, though only for a minute ahead, and through the déjà vu filter. Plus side effects.

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded:
They seem different enough. SCP-688 is for an unknown purpose and has an unknown amount of power. It is currently Euclid because it seems unlikely to destroy the world on its own. This one just seems to represent time. It only flows one way, and making it flow the other just rewinds time to before it was flipped.

Plus, this is a controlled effect. Keep it with you. If something goes wrong in a split-second, rewind time to fix. This much more horrifying in useable power, as it is unlikely to kill you.
